Similar example: In H₃O⁺, one O–H bond is dative, formed by oxygen's lone pair.
Tip: Dative bond: both shared electrons come from one atom.

questions.text: Which of the following molecules is linear in shape?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Molecular shape is decided by the number of bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom (VSEPR theory).
Step 1: CO₂: carbon has two double bonds and no lone pairs.
Step 2: Two regions of electron density repel each other to 180°.
Step 3: So CO₂ is linear (O=C=O).
Answer: CO₂.
Common mistake: H₂O has two lone pairs on oxygen so it is bent, not linear.
Similar example: BeCl₂ also has two bond pairs and no lone pairs, so it is linear.
Tip: Linear: 2 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs.

questions.text: The relative atomic mass of an element with isotopes of mass 35 (75%) and 37 (25%) is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the isotopic masses.
Step 1: RAM = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25)/100.
Step 2: = (2625 + 925)/100 = 3550/100.
Step 3: = 35.5.
Answer: 35.5.
Common mistake: Taking a simple average (35 + 37)/2 = 36 ignores the percentage abundance.
Similar example: Boron: 80% ¹¹B and 20% ¹⁰B gives (11 × 80 + 10 × 20)/100 = 10.8.
Tip: The answer should lie closer to the more abundant isotope.

questions.text: The gas used in the manufacture of ammonia by the Haber process is obtained from air by
questions.explanation:
Concept: Air is a mixture. Its components are separated by cooling it until it liquefies, then warming gradually.
Step 1: Air is filtered, then compressed and cooled until it becomes liquid.
Step 2: Nitrogen (b.p. −196°C) boils off before oxygen (b.p. −183°C).
Step 3: This is fractional distillation of liquid air.
Answer: fractional distillation of liquid air.
Similar example: Argon, neon and oxygen are also obtained from liquid air in this way.
Tip: Haber process: N₂ from liquid air, H₂ from natural gas.

questions.text: The permanent hardness of water can be removed by
questions.explanation:
Concept: Permanent hardness is due to dissolved sulphates and chlorides of calcium and magnesium, and boiling does not remove it.
Step 1: Add sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) (washing soda), Na₂CO₃.
Step 2: CO₃²⁻ precipitates the ions: Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → CaCO₃↓.
Step 3: The insoluble carbonate is filtered off, leaving soft water.
Answer: adding sodium trioxocarbonate(IV).
Common mistake: Boiling only removes temporary hardness, not permanent hardness.
Similar example: Magnesium sulphate hardness is removed the same way: Mg²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → MgCO₃↓.
Tip: Temporary: boiling. Permanent: washing soda or ion exchange.

questions.text: Hardness of water is caused by the presence of
questions.explanation:
Concept: Hard water does not form lather easily with soap because it contains certain dissolved metal ions.
Step 1: The ions are Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.
Step 2: They react with soap to form insoluble scum.
Step 3: Sodium and potassium salts of soap are soluble, so Na⁺ and K⁺ do not cause hardness.
Answer: calcium and magnesium ions.
Similar example: Calcium hydrogencarbonate causes temporary hardness and calcium sulphate causes permanent hardness.
Tip: Hardness = calcium and magnesium ions. Always.

questions.text: The solubility of a salt is 20 g per 100 g of water at 30°C. The mass of salt that will saturate 250 g of water at this temperature is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Solubility is the mass of solute that saturates 100 g of solvent at a given temperature.
Step 1: 20 g of salt saturates 100 g of water.
Step 2: Mass of water given = 250 g, which is 2.5 times 100 g.
Step 3: Mass of salt = 20 × 2.5 = 50 g.
Answer: 50 g.
Similar example: If solubility is 30 g per 100 g of water, then 200 g of water holds 30 × 2 = 60 g.
Tip: Set up a simple proportion: solute/water stays constant.

questions.text: Which of the following gases is mainly responsible for acid rain?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Acid rain is caused by acidic oxides of non-metals dissolving in rain water.
Step 1: SO₂ (from burning fossil fuels) dissolves in rain to give sulphurous acid and then sulphuric acid.
Step 2: Oxides of nitrogen give nitric acid.
Step 3: CO, N₂ and H₂ do not form strong acids.
Answer: SO₂.
Common mistake: CO₂ makes rain slightly acidic (pH ≈ 5.6), but SO₂ and NOₓ are the main cause of acid rain.
Similar example: Smelting sulphide ores releases SO₂, which is why areas near smelters suffer acid rain.
Tip: Acid rain: SO₂ and NOₓ.

questions.text: The pH of a solution of hydrochloric acid whose hydrogen ion concentration is 0.001 mol/dm³ is
questions.explanation:
Concept: pH = −log[H⁺].
Step 1: [H⁺] = 0.001 = 10⁻³ mol/dm³.
Step 2: pH = −log(10⁻³) = 3.
Answer: 3.
Similar example: If [H⁺] = 10⁻⁵ mol/dm³, pH = 5.
Tip: The power of 10 gives the pH directly when [H⁺] is an exact power of ten.

questions.text: What volume of 0.2 mol/dm³ NaOH is required to neutralise 25 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄?
questions.explanation:
Concept: For titration calculations, use the balanced equation and moles = concentration × volume (dm³).
Step 1: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.
Step 2: Moles of acid = 0.1 × 0.025 = 0.0025 mol.
Step 3: Moles of NaOH = 2 × 0.0025 = 0.005 mol.
Step 4: Volume of NaOH = 0.005 ÷ 0.2 = 0.025 dm³ = 25 cm³.
Answer: 25 cm³.
Common mistake: Forgetting the 2 in 2NaOH gives 12.5 cm³.
Similar example: 20 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl needs 20 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ NaOH, because the ratio is 1 : 1.
Tip: Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000.

questions.text: Which of the following salts is acidic in aqueous solution?
questions.explanation:
Concept: A salt hydrolyses in water according to the strengths of its parent acid and base.
Step 1: NH₄Cl comes from a strong acid (HCl) and a weak base (NH₃).
Step 2: NH₄⁺ reacts with water: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺.
Step 3: H₃O⁺ makes the solution acidic.
Answer: NH₄Cl.
Similar example: Na₂CO₃ comes from a strong base and a weak acid, so it is basic.
Tip: Strong acid + weak base gives an acidic salt. Strong base + weak acid gives a basic salt.

questions.text: The oxidation number of chromium in K₂Cr₂O₇ is
questions.explanation:
Concept: The sum of the oxidation numbers in a neutral compound is zero.
Step 1: K = +1, O = −2. Let Cr = x.
Step 2: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0.
Step 3: 2 + 2x − 14 = 0, so 2x = 12 and x = +6.
Answer: +6.
Similar example: In KMnO₄: +1 + x − 8 = 0 gives Mn = +7.
Tip: Fix K = +1 and O = −2 first, then solve for the unknown.

questions.text: In the reaction Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, the oxidising agent is
questions.explanation:
Concept: An oxidising agent gains electrons and is itself reduced.
Step 1: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (zinc is oxidised, so it is the reducing agent).
Step 2: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (copper ions gain electrons).
Step 3: So Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent.
Answer: Cu²⁺.
Common mistake: Zinc is the reducing agent, not the oxidising agent.
Similar example: In Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂, Cl₂ is the oxidising agent.
Tip: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

questions.text: During the electrolysis of dilute sulphuric acid using platinum electrodes, the gas liberated at the cathode is
questions.explanation:
Concept: In electrolysis, positive ions go to the cathode and gain electrons.
Step 1: Dilute H₂SO₄ contains H⁺, OH⁻ and SO₄²⁻ ions.
Step 2: At the cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
Step 3: So hydrogen gas is liberated at the cathode (oxygen at the anode).
Answer: hydrogen.
Common mistake: Oxygen is formed at the anode, not at the cathode.
Similar example: Electrolysis of water gives H₂ and O₂ in the volume ratio 2 : 1.
Tip: Cathode = reduction = metals or hydrogen.

questions.text: The quantity of electricity required to deposit 1 mole of copper from Cu²⁺ solution is [F = 96,500 C]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Faraday's law: the charge needed equals the number of electrons transferred × 96,500 C per mole of electrons.
Step 1: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
Step 2: 1 mole of Cu needs 2 mol of electrons = 2 F.
Step 3: Q = 2 × 96,500 = 193,000 C.
Answer: 193,000 C.
Common mistake: Using 96,500 C only is wrong because Cu²⁺ carries a 2+ charge.
Similar example: 1 mole of Ag from Ag⁺ needs 1 F = 96,500 C; 1 mole of Al needs 3 F = 289,500 C.
Tip: Charge = ion charge × 96,500 per mole.

questions.text: A reaction in which the enthalpy of the products is less than that of the reactants is
questions.explanation:
Concept: ΔH is the heat change of a reaction. ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants).
Step 1: Products have lower enthalpy than reactants, so ΔH is negative.
Step 2: Heat is released to the surroundings.
Step 3: Such a reaction is exothermic.
Answer: exothermic.
Similar example: Burning magnesium, neutralization and respiration are exothermic.
Tip: Negative ΔH = exothermic. Positive ΔH = endothermic.

questions.text: Given that ΔH for the combustion of carbon is −393 kJ/mol, how much heat is released when 6 g of carbon is burnt? [C = 12]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Heat released = number of moles × heat of combustion.
Step 1: Moles of carbon = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 mol.
Step 2: Heat = 0.5 × 393 = 196.5 kJ.
Answer: 196.5 kJ.
Common mistake: Giving 393 kJ is wrong because that is the heat for a full mole (12 g).
Similar example: Burning 24 g of carbon releases 2 × 393 = 786 kJ.
Tip: Convert the mass to moles first.

questions.text: Increasing the temperature of a reaction increases its rate because
options: more molecules possess the activation energy
questions.explanation:
Concept: Collision theory: a reaction occurs when particles collide with enough energy (the activation energy).
Step 1: Raising the temperature gives the particles more kinetic energy.
Step 2: A larger fraction of the particles has energy ≥ the activation energy.
Step 3: More collisions are effective, so the rate increases.
Answer: more molecules possess the activation energy.
Common mistake: Temperature does not lower the activation energy; only a catalyst does that.
Similar example: Food spoils faster in a hot kitchen than in a refrigerator.
Tip: Temperature: more energetic collisions. Concentration: more frequent collisions.

questions.text: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by
options: providing an alternative path with lower activation energy
questions.explanation:
Concept: A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction without being used up.
Step 1: It provides an alternative reaction pathway.
Step 2: This pathway has a lower activation energy.
Step 3: More particles can react, so the reaction is faster.
Answer: providing an alternative path with lower activation energy.
Common mistake: A catalyst does not change ΔH or the position of equilibrium.
Similar example: MnO₂ speeds up the decomposition of H₂O₂ by lowering the activation energy.
Tip: Catalyst: faster, not more product.

questions.text: In the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ. The yield of ammonia is increased by
questions.explanation:
Concept: Le Chatelier's principle: if you change the conditions of an equilibrium, it shifts to oppose the change.
Step 1: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles on the right.
Step 2: Raising the pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles.
Step 3: So the equilibrium moves right and the yield of NH₃ increases.
Answer: increasing the pressure.
Common mistake: Raising the temperature would favour the endothermic (reverse) reaction and reduce NH₃ yield, since the forward reaction is exothermic.
Similar example: For N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂, high pressure favours N₂O₄ (1 mole against 2).
Tip: Count moles of gas on each side before applying pressure arguments.

questions.text: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), the equilibrium constant expression Kc is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Kc = [products]^coefficients ÷ [reactants]^coefficients.
Step 1: Products: SO₃ with coefficient 2, so [SO₃]².
Step 2: Reactants: SO₂ with coefficient 2 and O₂ with coefficient 1.
Step 3: Kc = [SO₃]²/([SO₂]²[O₂]).
Answer: [SO₃]²/([SO₂]²[O₂]).
Common mistake: Do not multiply concentrations by the coefficients; raise them to the power of the coefficients.
Similar example: For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]).
Tip: Products on top, reactants at the bottom. Coefficients become powers.

questions.text: Concentrated sulphuric acid turns sugar black because it acts as a
questions.explanation:
Concept: Concentrated H₂SO₄ is a strong dehydrating agent. It removes water, or the elements H and O in the ratio 2 : 1, from compounds.
Step 1: Sugar is C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁.
Step 2: Concentrated H₂SO₄ removes 11 H₂O from it.
Step 3: Black carbon is left behind.
Answer: dehydrating agent.
Similar example: It also removes water from blue CuSO₄·5H₂O, turning it white.
Tip: Sugar turning black is the classic dehydration test.

questions.text: Which of the following gases bleaches moist litmus paper?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Chlorine is a bleaching gas. It acts only in the presence of water.
Step 1: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl.
Step 2: HOCl releases oxygen, which oxidises the dye.
Step 3: So moist litmus paper is bleached.
Answer: Chlorine.
Common mistake: Dry chlorine does not bleach dry litmus paper.
Similar example: SO₂ also bleaches, but by reduction, and the colour may return.
Tip: Chlorine first turns litmus red, then bleaches it white.

questions.text: The metal that reacts with cold water only very slowly but vigorously with steam is
questions.explanation:
Concept: The reactivity series decides how a metal reacts with water.
Step 1: Na and K react vigorously with cold water.
Step 2: Mg reacts very slowly with cold water but burns in steam: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂.
Step 3: Cu does not react with water or steam.
Answer: magnesium.
Similar example: Zinc and iron react with steam but not with cold water.
Tip: Order: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au.

questions.text: The most abundant ore of aluminium is
questions.explanation:
Concept: An ore is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably.
Step 1: The ore of aluminium is bauxite, Al₂O₃·2H₂O.
Step 2: Haematite is iron ore, galena is lead ore and cassiterite is tin ore.
Answer: bauxite.
Similar example: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of purified bauxite dissolved in molten cryolite.
Tip: Bauxite = Al. Haematite = Fe. Galena = Pb. Cassiterite = Sn.

questions.text: The IUPAC name of the compound CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is
questions.explanation:
Concept: IUPAC naming: find the longest carbon chain, name it, then name and number the branches.
Step 1: The longest chain has 4 carbons: butane.
Step 2: A CH₃ branch is on the second carbon: 2-methyl.
Step 3: The name is 2-methylbutane.
Answer: 2-methylbutane.
Common mistake: Choosing the chain incorrectly (counting the branch) gives wrong names such as pentane.
Similar example: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃ has a 3-carbon chain with a methyl on C-2: 2-methylpropane.
Tip: Number from the end that gives the branch the lowest number.

questions.text: Which of the following is an unsaturated hydrocarbon?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain C=C or C≡C bonds. Alkenes follow CₙH₂ₙ.
Step 1: Alkanes: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. C₃H₈, C₄H₁₀ and CH₄ are saturated.
Step 2: C₃H₆ fits CₙH₂ₙ, so it is an alkene (propene).
Step 3: It therefore has a C=C bond.
Answer: C₃H₆.
Similar example: C₂H₄ fits CₙH₂ₙ: ethene, unsaturated.
Tip: Test: if H = 2C + 2, saturated alkane. If fewer, unsaturated.

questions.text: The reaction of ethene with bromine water is an example of
questions.explanation:
Concept: Alkenes undergo addition reactions across the C=C bond.
Step 1: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂Br–CH₂Br.
Step 2: Two substances combine into one product, so it is addition.
Step 3: The orange bromine water is decolourised.
Answer: addition reaction.
Common mistake: Alkanes undergo substitution, not addition.
Similar example: Ethene + H₂ → ethane (hydrogenation) is also addition.
Tip: Bromine water decolourised: unsaturation.

questions.text: The functional group present in alkanols is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Functional groups give a homologous series its properties.
Step 1: The functional group of alkanols (alcohols) is the hydroxyl group –OH.
Step 2: –COOH belongs to alkanoic acids, –CHO to alkanals and –CO– to alkanones.
Answer: –OH.
Similar example: Ethanol is CH₃CH₂OH and ethanoic acid is CH₃COOH.
Tip: Alkanol = –OH. Alkanoic acid = –COOH.

questions.text: Ethanol can be converted into ethene by
options: heating with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ at 170°C
questions.explanation:
Concept: Dehydration removes a molecule of water from an alcohol.
Step 1: Heat ethanol with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 170°C.
Step 2: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O.
Step 3: Ethene is formed.
Answer: heating with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ at 170°C.
Common mistake: At a lower temperature (about 140°C) with excess alcohol, you get diethyl ether, not ethene.
Similar example: Propanol dehydrates to propene in the same way.
Tip: Excess acid and 170°C: alkene.

questions.text: The process by which an ester is hydrolysed by an alkali to produce soap is called
questions.explanation:
Concept: Saponification is the alkaline hydrolysis of fats and oils.
Step 1: Fat or oil (an ester) + NaOH → soap + glycerol.
Step 2: The sodium salt of the fatty acid is the soap.
Answer: saponification.
Common mistake: Esterification is the opposite: acid + alcohol → ester + water.
Similar example: Boiling palm oil with caustic soda is how local soap is made.
Tip: Saponification = soap-making.

questions.text: Which of the following will turn acidified potassium dichromate(VI) from orange to green?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ is an oxidising agent that changes colour when it oxidises something.
Step 1: Ethanol is oxidised to ethanal and then ethanoic acid.
Step 2: Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) is reduced to Cr³⁺ (green).
Step 3: So only ethanol turns the solution green.
Answer: Ethanol.
Common mistake: Alkanes such as ethane do not reduce the dichromate and so cause no colour change.
Similar example: Breathalysers use this reaction to detect ethanol on the breath.
Tip: Orange → green means something was oxidised.

questions.text: A mixture of ethanol (b.p. 78°C) and water (b.p. 100°C) is best separated by
questions.explanation:
Concept: Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with different boiling points.
Step 1: Ethanol boils at 78°C and water at 100°C.
Step 2: On heating, the more volatile ethanol vaporises first and rises up the fractionating column.
Step 3: It condenses and is collected, while water remains behind.
Answer: fractional distillation.
Common mistake: Simple distillation separates a liquid from a non-volatile solid, but the boiling points here are not far enough apart for it to work well.
Similar example: Separating liquid nitrogen from liquid oxygen in liquid air uses the same principle.
Tip: Two miscible liquids: fractional distillation.

questions.text: Which of the following is used to separate the components of crude oil?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different boiling ranges.
Step 1: Crude oil is heated and fed into a fractionating tower.
Step 2: Fractions with low boiling points (petrol, kerosene) rise to the top.
Step 3: Heavy fractions (diesel, lubricating oil, bitumen) collect near the bottom.
Answer: Fractional distillation.
Similar example: Refinery gas, petrol, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil and bitumen are the common fractions.
Tip: The higher the boiling point, the lower the fraction leaves the tower.

questions.text: The substance whose boiling and melting points are sharp and fixed is
questions.explanation:
Concept: A pure substance has fixed physical properties; a mixture does not.
Step 1: A pure substance melts and boils at a single sharp temperature.
Step 2: A mixture melts or boils over a range of temperatures.
Step 3: Therefore a sharp, fixed melting and boiling point shows a pure substance.
Answer: a pure substance.
Similar example: Impure ice melts below 0°C. Pure ice melts at exactly 0°C.
Tip: Melting-point tests check purity.

questions.text: Carbon combines with 32 g of oxygen to form CO₂ while hydrogen combines with 8 g of oxygen per 1 g of hydrogen in H₂O, and carbon combines with 4 g of hydrogen in CH₄ per 12 g of carbon. This is evidence for the law of
questions.explanation:
Concept: Law of reciprocal proportions: if two elements each combine with a fixed mass of a third element, they combine with each other in the same ratio or a simple multiple of it.
Step 1: H : O in water = 1 : 8.
Step 2: C : O in CO₂ = 12 : 32 = 3 : 8.
Step 3: Predicted C : H = 3 : 1.
Step 4: In CH₄, C : H = 12 : 4 = 3 : 1, which matches.
Answer: reciprocal proportions.
Common mistake: Multiple proportions compare the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of another in two different compounds. That is not the case here.
Similar example: Law of reciprocal proportions is also called the law of equivalent proportions.
Tip: Three elements, two compounds each with the third: reciprocal proportions.

questions.text: What is the mass of 0.25 mole of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), CaCO₃? [Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Mass = moles × molar mass.
Step 1: Molar mass of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + 3(16) = 100 g/mol.
Step 2: Mass = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g.
Answer: 25 g.
Common mistake: Using 1 mole instead of 0.25 mole gives 100 g.
Similar example: Mass of 2 moles of NaOH (40 g/mol) = 80 g.
Tip: Add up the atomic masses carefully before multiplying.

questions.text: Calculate the number of molecules in 1.8 g of water. [H = 1, O = 16, Avogadro constant = 6.0 × 10²³]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Number of molecules = moles × Avogadro's number (6.0 × 10²³).
Step 1: Molar mass of H₂O = 2(1) + 16 = 18 g/mol.
Step 2: Moles = 1.8 ÷ 18 = 0.1 mol.
Step 3: Molecules = 0.1 × 6.0 × 10²³ = 6.0 × 10²².
Answer: 6.0 × 10²².
Similar example: 9 g of water = 0.5 mol = 3.0 × 10²³ molecules.
Tip: Mass → moles → particles.

questions.text: A gas occupies 500 cm³ at 2 atm. What volume will it occupy at 4 atm at the same temperature?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
Step 1: P₁ = 2 atm, V₁ = 500 cm³, P₂ = 4 atm.
Step 2: V₂ = (2 × 500) ÷ 4.
Step 3: V₂ = 250 cm³.
Answer: 250 cm³.
Common mistake: Doubling the pressure halves the volume. It does not double it.
Similar example: A gas at 1 atm and 100 cm³ is compressed to 5 atm: V = 20 cm³.
Tip: Pressure up means volume down at constant temperature.

questions.text: The kinetic theory of gases assumes that gas molecules
options: are in constant random motion and have negligible volume
questions.explanation:
Concept: The kinetic theory describes an ideal gas as a large number of tiny particles in rapid motion.
Step 1: The molecules move constantly and randomly.
Step 2: Their own volume is negligible compared with the container volume.
Step 3: Collisions are perfectly elastic, so no energy is lost.
Answer: are in constant random motion and have negligible volume.
Common mistake: Gas molecules have negligible attraction for each other. Strong attraction applies to liquids and solids.
Similar example: Real gases deviate from this model at high pressure and low temperature.
Tip: Gas particles: random, tiny, elastic, no attraction.

questions.text: At s.t.p., the volume occupied by 8 g of oxygen gas is [O = 16, molar volume = 22.4 dm³]
questions.explanation:
Concept: At s.t.p., 1 mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm³.
Step 1: Molar mass of O₂ = 32 g/mol.
Step 2: Moles = 8 ÷ 32 = 0.25 mol.
Step 3: Volume = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 dm³.
Answer: 5.6 dm³.
Common mistake: Using 16 g/mol for O₂ would give 11.2 dm³, which is wrong.
Similar example: 16 g of O₂ = 0.5 mol, which occupies 11.2 dm³.
Tip: Moles first, then × 22.4.

questions.text: The number of neutrons in ²³₁₁Na is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Neutron number = mass number − atomic number.
Step 1: ²³₁₁Na has mass number 23 and atomic number 11.
Step 2: Neutrons = 23 − 11 = 12.
Answer: 12.
Similar example: ³⁵₁₇Cl has 35 − 17 = 18 neutrons.
Tip: Top number: mass. Bottom number: protons.

questions.text: Isotopes of an element have the same
questions.explanation:
Concept: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
Step 1: Same element means same atomic number.
Step 2: Atomic number equals the number of protons.
Step 3: So isotopes have the same number of protons but different mass numbers.
Answer: number of protons.
Common mistake: Neutrons and mass number are what differ in isotopes.
Similar example: ¹²C and ¹⁴C both have 6 protons but 6 and 8 neutrons.
Tip: Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons.

questions.text: Which of the following has the highest first ionization energy?
questions.explanation:
Concept: First ionization energy is the energy needed to remove one electron from a gaseous atom.
Step 1: Ionization energy increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Step 2: Helium has its two electrons in the first shell, close to the nucleus.
Step 3: So He has the highest first ionization energy of all elements.
Answer: Helium.
Similar example: Order for noble gases: He > Ne > Ar.
Tip: Small atom + full outer shell = very high ionization energy.

questions.text: The bond formed when two atoms each contribute one electron to a shared pair is called
questions.explanation:
Concept: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
Step 1: Each atom contributes one electron to the shared pair.
Step 2: If one atom supplies both electrons, it is a dative bond.
Step 3: Ionic bonds involve transfer of electrons.
Answer: covalent bond.
Similar example: In Cl₂, each chlorine contributes one electron to make a single covalent bond.
Tip: Share = covalent. Transfer = ionic.

questions.text: The high boiling point of water compared with hydrogen sulphide is due to
questions.explanation:
Concept: Hydrogen bonding is a strong intermolecular force between H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on a neighbouring molecule.
Step 1: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other.
Step 2: Extra energy is needed to break these bonds.
Step 3: H₂S has no hydrogen bonds, so it boils at a much lower temperature.
Answer: hydrogen bonding.
Similar example: NH₃ and HF also have unusually high boiling points because of hydrogen bonding.
Tip: H bonded to N, O or F means hydrogen bonding.

questions.text: Which of the following elements is a member of Group 17 of the periodic table?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons.
Step 1: Group 17 (the halogens) elements have 7 outer electrons.
Step 2: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are the members.
Step 3: Chlorine (2, 8, 7) is in Group 17.
Answer: Chlorine.
Common mistake: Argon is in Group 18 (noble gases) and sodium is in Group 1.
Similar example: Sulphur (2, 8, 6) is in Group 16.
Tip: Outer electrons tell you the group.

questions.text: Which gas constitutes about 78% by volume of dry air?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Dry air is mainly nitrogen and oxygen.
Step 1: Nitrogen: about 78%.
Step 2: Oxygen: about 21%.
Step 3: Argon, carbon(IV) oxide and others make up about 1%.
Answer: Nitrogen.
Common mistake: Oxygen is the second most abundant gas, not the most abundant.
Similar example: Argon is about 0.9% and CO₂ about 0.03% of air.
Tip: 78 : 21 : 1 for N₂ : O₂ : others.

questions.text: Water of crystallization is the water that
options: is chemically combined in the crystals of a salt
is lost on exposure to air by every salt
has no effect on crystal shape
questions.explanation:
Concept: Water of crystallization is water molecules chemically bound in a crystal.
Step 1: CuSO₄·5H₂O has five water molecules in each formula unit.
Step 2: Heating drives the water off and leaves anhydrous CuSO₄ (white).
Step 3: The crystal shape and colour depend on this water.
Answer: is chemically combined in the crystals of a salt.
Similar example: Washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
Tip: Blue CuSO₄·5H₂O → white CuSO₄ on heating.

questions.text: A substance that absorbs moisture from the air and dissolves in it is said to be
questions.explanation:
Concept: Deliquescent substances absorb water from the air until they dissolve.
Step 1: Deliquescent: absorbs enough moisture to form a solution (e.g. NaOH, CaCl₂, FeCl₃).
Step 2: Efflorescent: loses water of crystallization to the air (e.g. washing soda).
Step 3: Hygroscopic: absorbs moisture but may not dissolve.
Answer: deliquescent.
Similar example: NaOH pellets left in the open become wet and sticky.
Tip: Deliquescent = dissolves. Efflorescent = dries.

questions.text: The solubility curve of most solid solutes in water shows that solubility
questions.explanation:
Concept: A solubility curve plots solubility against temperature.
Step 1: For most solids, the curve slopes upwards.
Step 2: So solubility increases as temperature increases.
Step 3: Exceptions such as Ca(OH)₂ and gases decrease with rising temperature.
Answer: increases with temperature.
Similar example: KNO₃ has a steep upward curve; NaCl is almost flat.
Tip: Solids: usually soluble hot. Gases: soluble cold.

questions.text: Carbon(II) oxide is poisonous because it
options: reacts with water to form an acid
combines with haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does
questions.explanation:
Concept: Carbon(II) oxide (CO) is a colourless, odourless, toxic gas.
Step 1: Haemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood.
Step 2: CO binds to haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen does.
Step 3: The blood can no longer carry enough oxygen, and the person may die.
Answer: combines with haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does.
Similar example: Burning charcoal in a closed room can lead to CO poisoning.
Tip: CO comes from incomplete combustion.

questions.text: Which of the following is a primary pollutant?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Primary pollutants are emitted directly from a source. Secondary pollutants are formed later by reactions in the atmosphere.
Step 1: CO is released directly from exhaust pipes and fires.
Step 2: Ozone in smog, PAN and sulphuric acid mist are formed by secondary reactions.
Answer: Carbon(II) oxide.
Similar example: SO₂ from factory chimneys is primary; the H₂SO₄ it forms in rain is secondary.
Tip: Direct emission = primary.

questions.text: A solution has a hydroxide ion concentration of 1 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³. Its pH is
questions.explanation:
Concept: pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C, and pOH = −log[OH⁻].
Step 1: [OH⁻] = 10⁻³ mol/dm³, so pOH = 3.
Step 2: pH = 14 − 3 = 11.
Answer: 11.
Common mistake: Giving 3 is wrong because that is the pOH, not the pH.
Similar example: [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁵ mol/dm³ gives pOH = 5 and pH = 9.
Tip: For bases, find pOH first, then subtract from 14.

questions.text: The conjugate base of H₂O in the equilibrium H₂O + NH₃ ⇌ OH⁻ + NH₄⁺ is
questions.explanation:
Concept: A conjugate pair differs by one proton (H⁺). An acid donates a proton and the species left is its conjugate base.
Step 1: In H₂O + NH₃ ⇌ OH⁻ + NH₄⁺, water donates H⁺ to NH₃.
Step 2: Water becomes OH⁻.
Step 3: So OH⁻ is the conjugate base of H₂O.
Answer: OH⁻.
Similar example: The conjugate base of HCl is Cl⁻.
Tip: Acid − H⁺ = conjugate base.

questions.text: Which of the following oxides reacts with both dilute acids and strong alkalis to form a salt and water?
questions.explanation:
Concept: An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and bases.
Step 1: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O (acts as a base).
Step 2: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄ (acts as an acid).
Step 3: Na₂O is basic. CO₂ and SO₃ are acidic.
Answer: Al₂O₃.
Similar example: ZnO and PbO are also amphoteric.
Tip: Amphoteric oxides: Al₂O₃, ZnO, PbO.

questions.text: Which indicator is most suitable for the titration of a strong acid against a weak base?
questions.explanation:
Concept: The indicator must change colour at the pH of the equivalence point.
Step 1: A strong acid with a weak base gives an acidic salt at the equivalence point (pH below 7).
Step 2: Methyl orange changes colour in the acidic range (pH 3.1–4.4).
Step 3: So methyl orange is the suitable indicator.
Answer: Methyl orange.
Common mistake: Phenolphthalein is for a weak acid with a strong base.
Similar example: Strong acid with strong base: either indicator works.
Tip: Weak base: methyl orange. Weak acid: phenolphthalein.

questions.text: The oxidation number of manganese in KMnO₄ is
questions.explanation:
Concept: The sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound is zero.
Step 1: K = +1, O = −2. Let Mn = x.
Step 2: +1 + x + 4(−2) = 0.
Step 3: x = +7.
Answer: +7.
Similar example: Mn in MnO₂: x − 4 = 0 gives +4.
Tip: Mn can be +2, +4, +6 or +7.

questions.text: Which of the following reactions is a redox reaction?
questions.explanation:
Concept: A redox reaction involves a change in oxidation numbers.
Step 1: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO: Mg goes from 0 to +2 (oxidised) and O goes from 0 to −2 (reduced).
Step 2: NaOH + HCl and AgNO₃ + NaCl involve no change in oxidation numbers.
Step 3: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ is thermal decomposition with no change in oxidation numbers.
Answer: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
Similar example: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu is also a redox reaction.
Tip: Check whether any element changes oxidation number.

questions.text: In electroplating a spoon with silver, the spoon is made the
questions.explanation:
Concept: In electroplating, the object to be plated is the cathode, because metal ions gain electrons there.
Step 1: The anode is the plating metal (silver).
Step 2: The electrolyte contains Ag⁺ ions.
Step 3: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag deposits on the spoon, which is the cathode.
Answer: cathode.
Similar example: To nickel-plate a key, the key is the cathode and the anode is nickel.
Tip: Plate at the cathode.

questions.text: When a current of 2 A is passed through a solution for 965 seconds, the quantity of electricity used is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Quantity of charge Q = current (A) × time (s).
Step 1: I = 2 A, t = 965 s.
Step 2: Q = 2 × 965 = 1930 C.
Answer: 1930 C.
Similar example: 3 A for 100 s gives 300 C.
Tip: Convert minutes to seconds first.

questions.text: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burnt in oxygen is called enthalpy of
questions.explanation:
Concept: Standard enthalpy changes have specific names.
Step 1: Enthalpy of combustion: heat change when 1 mole of a substance is completely burnt in oxygen.
Step 2: Enthalpy of formation: 1 mole of a compound formed from its elements.
Step 3: Enthalpy of neutralization: 1 mole of water formed from an acid and a base.
Answer: combustion.
Similar example: C + O₂ → CO₂ ΔH = −393 kJ is the enthalpy of combustion of carbon.
Tip: Burn one mole in oxygen: combustion.

questions.text: Which of the following processes is endothermic?
questions.explanation:
Concept: An endothermic process absorbs heat from the surroundings.
Step 1: Evaporation needs heat to turn liquid into vapour.
Step 2: Condensation, freezing and burning release heat.
Step 3: So only evaporation is endothermic.
Answer: Evaporation of water.
Similar example: Melting of ice is also endothermic.
Tip: Endothermic: surroundings get colder.

questions.text: The rate of reaction between marble chips and dilute HCl can be increased by
options: using a larger lump of marble
questions.explanation:
Concept: Rate increases with surface area because more particles are exposed to collisions.
Step 1: Powdered marble has a larger surface area than lumps.
Step 2: More collisions occur per second.
Step 3: So the reaction is faster.
Answer: using powdered marble.
Common mistake: Lowering the temperature or diluting the acid would slow the reaction.
Similar example: Powdered zinc reacts faster with acid than zinc granules.
Tip: Smaller particles: faster rate.

questions.text: The rate law for a reaction is rate = k[A]²[B]. The overall order of the reaction is
questions.explanation:
Concept: The order of a reaction is the sum of the powers of the concentrations in the rate law.
Step 1: Rate = k[A]²[B].
Step 2: Order in A = 2, order in B = 1.
Step 3: Overall order = 2 + 1 = 3.
Answer: 3.
Similar example: Rate = k[A][B] is second order overall.
Tip: Add the powers.

questions.text: According to Le Chatelier's principle, if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the system will
options: shift in the direction of the disturbance
shift in the direction that opposes the disturbance
questions.explanation:
Concept: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium responds to oppose any change imposed on it.
Step 1: If you add reactant, the equilibrium shifts to use it up.
Step 2: If you raise the temperature, it shifts in the endothermic direction.
Step 3: If you raise the pressure, it shifts to the side with fewer gas moles.
Answer: shift in the direction that opposes the disturbance.
Similar example: Removing NH₃ from the Haber process pushes the equilibrium to the right.
Tip: The system resists the change.

questions.text: A catalyst has no effect on the position of equilibrium because it
options: speeds up forward and backward reactions equally
questions.explanation:
Concept: A catalyst speeds up both forward and backward reactions by the same factor.
Step 1: It lowers the activation energy of both directions equally.
Step 2: Equilibrium is reached sooner.
Step 3: The equilibrium composition and the value of Kc do not change.
Answer: speeds up forward and backward reactions equally.
Similar example: Iron in the Haber process only speeds up how fast equilibrium is reached.
Tip: Catalyst: faster, not more.

questions.text: The catalyst used in the contact process for sulphuric acid manufacture is
questions.explanation:
Concept: The contact process makes sulphuric acid in three steps: burn S to SO₂, oxidise SO₂ to SO₃, then absorb SO₃.
Step 1: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ is carried out at about 450°C.
Step 2: The catalyst is vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅.
Step 3: SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ to form oleum.
Answer: vanadium(V) oxide.
Common mistake: Iron is used in the Haber process and platinum in the Ostwald process.
Similar example: Three industrial processes and their catalysts: Haber (Fe), Contact (V₂O₅), Ostwald (Pt).
Tip: Contact = vanadium.

questions.text: Which of the following metals is extracted by the electrolysis of its molten ore?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Very reactive metals are extracted by electrolysis of their molten compounds.
Step 1: Sodium is extracted by electrolysis of molten NaCl (Downs cell).
Step 2: Iron and lead are extracted by reduction with carbon.
Step 3: Copper is often extracted by roasting and reduction.
Answer: Sodium.
Similar example: Aluminium is also extracted by electrolysis (of bauxite in molten cryolite).
Tip: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al: electrolysis.

questions.text: The general formula of alkanes is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons and follow the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Step 1: Methane (n = 1): CH₄. Ethane (n = 2): C₂H₆.
Step 2: Alkenes follow CₙH₂ₙ and alkynes follow CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.
Answer: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Similar example: Octane (n = 8) is C₈H₁₈.
Tip: Alkane: 2n + 2. Alkene: 2n. Alkyne: 2n − 2.

questions.text: Which of the following is the product of the complete combustion of ethanol?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Complete combustion of organic compounds produces carbon(IV) oxide and water.
Step 1: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
Step 2: Incomplete combustion gives CO or soot instead.
Answer: CO₂ and H₂O.
Similar example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
Tip: Plenty of oxygen: CO₂ and H₂O.

questions.text: Ethyne reacts with ammoniacal silver nitrate to give a precipitate. This confirms the presence of
questions.explanation:
Concept: Terminal alkynes (R–C≡C–H) have an acidic hydrogen on the triple-bonded carbon.
Step 1: Ethyne reacts with ammoniacal silver nitrate.
Step 2: The hydrogen is replaced by silver, giving a white precipitate of silver acetylide.
Step 3: This test shows a terminal triple bond.
Answer: a terminal triple bond.
Common mistake: Alkenes and alkanes do not give this precipitate.
Similar example: But-2-yne has no terminal hydrogen and gives no precipitate.
Tip: Precipitate with ammoniacal AgNO₃: terminal alkyne.

questions.text: Which of the following techniques is used to separate a mixture of coloured dyes?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Chromatography separates substances according to how fast they move through a stationary phase carried by a solvent.
Step 1: Place a spot of the dye mixture on filter paper and dip the edge in solvent.
Step 2: The solvent rises and carries each dye at a different speed, depending on its solubility and attraction to the paper.
Step 3: The dyes separate into distinct spots.
Answer: Chromatography.
Similar example: Chromatography is used to identify the colours in ink or to detect banned drugs in a sample.
Tip: Coloured mixtures and small amounts: chromatography.

questions.text: Which of the following is a heterogeneous mixture?
questions.explanation:
Concept: A heterogeneous mixture has visibly different phases. A homogeneous mixture looks the same throughout.
Step 1: Oil and water form two layers.
Step 2: Brine, air and sugar solution are uniform solutions.
Answer: Oil and water.
Similar example: Sand in water and chalk in water are also heterogeneous.
Tip: If you can see the boundary, it is heterogeneous.

questions.text: Which of the following compounds contains the highest percentage of nitrogen by mass? [N = 14, H = 1, C = 12, O = 16]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Percentage of an element = (mass of the element in the formula ÷ molar mass) × 100.
Step 1: Urea, CO(NH₂)₂: M = 12 + 16 + 2(14 + 2) = 60. N = 28/60 = 46.7%.
Step 2: NH₄Cl: M = 53.5. N = 14/53.5 = 26.2%.
Step 3: NaNO₃: M = 85. N = 14/85 = 16.5%.
Step 4: (NH₄)₂SO₄: M = 132. N = 28/132 = 21.2%.
Step 5: Urea has the highest nitrogen content.
Answer: Urea, CO(NH₂)₂.
Common mistake: Do not compare the number of nitrogen atoms. Compare the percentage by mass.
Similar example: NH₄NO₃ has 28/80 = 35% nitrogen, which is lower than urea.
Tip: Urea is the most nitrogen-rich common fertiliser.

questions.text: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon. Its empirical formula is [C = 12, H = 1]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Divide each percentage by the atomic mass, then divide by the smallest value.
Step 1: H = 100 − 85.7 = 14.3%.
Step 2: C = 85.7/12 = 7.14; H = 14.3/1 = 14.3.
Step 3: Divide by 7.14: C = 1, H = 2.
Step 4: Empirical formula: CH₂.
Answer: CH₂.
Similar example: A compound with 92.3% C and 7.7% H: C = 7.69, H = 7.7, so CH.
Tip: When a hydrocarbon's percentages are given, H = 100 − %C.

questions.text: What is the concentration in mol/dm³ of a solution containing 4.0 g of NaOH in 500 cm³ of solution? [Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume in dm³.
Step 1: Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g/mol.
Step 2: Moles = 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.1 mol.
Step 3: Volume = 500 cm³ = 0.5 dm³.
Step 4: Concentration = 0.1 ÷ 0.5 = 0.2 mol/dm³.
Answer: 0.2 mol/dm³.
Common mistake: Using 500 instead of 0.5 gives a wrong concentration. Convert cm³ to dm³.
Similar example: 2 g of NaOH in 250 cm³: 0.05 mol ÷ 0.25 dm³ = 0.2 mol/dm³.
Tip: Divide cm³ by 1000 for dm³.

questions.text: The mass of zinc that will react completely with 100 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ HCl is [Zn = 65]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Use the balanced equation to link moles of acid and zinc.
Step 1: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.
Step 2: Moles of HCl = 1.0 × 0.1 = 0.1 mol.
Step 3: Moles of Zn = 0.1 ÷ 2 = 0.05 mol.
Step 4: Mass of Zn = 0.05 × 65 = 3.25 g.
Answer: 3.25 g.
Common mistake: Forgetting the 2 in 2HCl gives 6.5 g.
Similar example: 0.2 mol of HCl reacts with 0.1 mol of Zn = 6.5 g.
Tip: Ratio from the equation, then convert.

questions.text: If 20 cm³ of a gas diffuses in 10 s, how long will 20 cm³ of a gas four times as dense take to diffuse under the same conditions?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Graham's law: time taken is proportional to the square root of the density (or molar mass).
Step 1: t₂/t₁ = √(ρ₂/ρ₁) = √4 = 2.
Step 2: t₂ = 2 × 10 = 20 s.
Answer: 20 s.
Common mistake: Do not multiply the time by 4. The relationship uses the square root.
Similar example: A gas 9 times as dense takes 3 times as long to diffuse.
Tip: Heavier gas: slower, by the square root factor.

questions.text: A given mass of gas occupies 600 cm³ at 27°C and 760 mmHg. What is its volume at s.t.p.?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Combine the temperature and pressure conditions. Pressure is constant here, so use Charles' law.
Step 1: At s.t.p., T = 273 K and P = 760 mmHg.
Step 2: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K.
Step 3: V₂ = 600 × 273/300 = 546 cm³.
Answer: 546 cm³.
Common mistake: Convert °C to kelvin before using the gas laws.
Similar example: A gas of 400 cm³ at 27°C has volume 364 cm³ at 0°C.
Tip: Pressure already at 760 mmHg means only temperature changes the volume.

questions.text: The pressure exerted by a mixture of gases is the sum of the pressures each gas would exert alone. This is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Dalton's law of partial pressures: the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of each gas.
Step 1: P(total) = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + …
Step 2: Each gas behaves as if it alone occupied the container.
Answer: Dalton's law of partial pressures.
Common mistake: Boyle's law relates pressure and volume of a single gas. Graham's law is about diffusion.
Similar example: If O₂ exerts 0.2 atm and N₂ 0.8 atm, the total pressure is 1.0 atm.
Tip: Dalton = partial pressures add.

questions.text: The electronic configuration of the chloride ion, Cl⁻, is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Electrons fill 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p in order. A negative ion has extra electrons.
Step 1: Cl has 17 electrons: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵.
Step 2: Cl⁻ gains one electron, so 18 electrons.
Step 3: Cl⁻: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶, the same as argon.
Answer: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶.
Common mistake: Writing 3p⁵ is the configuration of the chlorine atom, not the ion.
Similar example: Na⁺ has 10 electrons: 1s²2s²2p⁶.
Tip: Add electrons for negative ions, remove for positive ions.

questions.text: The shape of the ammonia molecule is
questions.explanation:
Concept: VSEPR: lone pairs repel more than bond pairs, so they squeeze the bond angles.
Step 1: Nitrogen in NH₃ has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair.
Step 2: 4 electron pairs arrange tetrahedrally but the lone pair is not part of the shape.
Step 3: The molecule is pyramidal (trigonal pyramid) with bond angle about 107°.
Answer: pyramidal.
Similar example: H₂O (2 bond pairs, 2 lone pairs) is bent with about 104.5°.
Tip: NH₃: 3 + 1 = pyramidal.

questions.text: Which of the following compounds has the highest melting point?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Ionic compounds have giant lattices with strong electrostatic attraction between ions.
Step 1: A lot of energy is needed to break the lattice.
Step 2: CH₄ and CO₂ are small covalent molecules with weak forces between molecules.
Step 3: H₂O has hydrogen bonds but they are weaker than ionic bonds.
Step 4: NaCl has the highest melting point (about 801°C).
Answer: NaCl.
Similar example: MgO melts at about 2850°C, higher than NaCl, because Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have larger charges.
Tip: Giant ionic or giant covalent: high melting point.

questions.text: Metals conduct electricity because of
options: the presence of mobile delocalized electrons
questions.explanation:
Concept: Metals have positive ions in a sea of delocalized electrons.
Step 1: When a voltage is applied, the free electrons move through the metal.
Step 2: This flow of electrons is an electric current.
Step 3: No ions move in a solid metal.
Answer: the presence of mobile delocalized electrons.
Common mistake: In molten salts and solutions, ions carry the current, not in metals.
Similar example: Graphite also conducts because of delocalized electrons.
Tip: Metals: electrons carry charge. Electrolytes: ions carry charge.

questions.text: In the periodic table, atomic radius generally
questions.explanation:
Concept: Atomic radius depends on nuclear charge and number of shells.
Step 1: Across a period, the nuclear charge increases but the number of shells stays the same.
Step 2: The outer electrons are pulled closer.
Step 3: Therefore atomic radius decreases across a period.
Answer: decreases across a period.
Common mistake: Down a group, atomic radius increases because new shells are added.
Similar example: Na (186 pm) is larger than Cl (99 pm).
Tip: Across: smaller. Down: bigger.

questions.text: The combustion of a fuel in a limited supply of oxygen leads mainly to
questions.explanation:
Concept: The products of burning depend on the supply of oxygen.
Step 1: Plenty of oxygen: complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O.
Step 2: Limited oxygen: incomplete combustion gives CO (and soot, C).
Step 3: CO is dangerous because it is toxic.
Answer: carbon(II) oxide.
Similar example: 2C + O₂ → 2CO shows incomplete combustion of carbon.
Tip: Poor ventilation produces CO.

questions.text: The ability of water to dissolve many substances is due to its
questions.explanation:
Concept: Water molecules are polar: oxygen is slightly negative and hydrogen is slightly positive.
Step 1: Water molecules surround ions and pull them away from the crystal (hydration).
Step 2: Polar and ionic substances therefore dissolve well.
Step 3: This is why water is called the universal solvent.
Answer: polar nature.
Similar example: Oil does not dissolve in water because oil is non-polar.
Tip: Like dissolves like.

questions.text: The solubility of a gas in a liquid generally
questions.explanation:
Concept: Gas solubility depends on temperature and pressure.
Step 1: Dissolving a gas releases heat, so raising the temperature reduces solubility.
Step 2: Raising the pressure increases solubility (Henry's law).
Step 3: Hot soft drinks lose their fizz faster.
Answer: decreases with increasing temperature.
Similar example: Fish struggle in warm water because it holds less dissolved oxygen.
Tip: Gases: solubility falls as temperature rises.

questions.text: In a saturated solution at constant temperature, the solute
options: is in dynamic equilibrium with the undissolved solute
has a lower concentration than the maximum
questions.explanation:
Concept: In a saturated solution, undissolved solute and dissolved solute are in dynamic equilibrium.
Step 1: Solute dissolves at a certain rate.
Step 2: Solute crystallizes at the same rate.
Step 3: So the amount dissolved stays constant.
Answer: is in dynamic equilibrium with the undissolved solute.
Similar example: Adding more solute to a saturated solution at the same temperature just settles at the bottom.
Tip: Saturated: no more dissolves.

questions.text: Eutrophication of water bodies is mainly caused by excess
questions.explanation:
Concept: Eutrophication is excessive growth of algae in water because of too many nutrients.
Step 1: Fertilizers and detergents wash into rivers and carry phosphates and nitrates.
Step 2: Algae multiply rapidly (algal bloom).
Step 3: When algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the oxygen.
Step 4: Fish die from lack of oxygen.
Answer: phosphates and nitrates.
Similar example: Run-off from farms is a common cause of eutrophication in lakes.
Tip: Phosphates + nitrates = nutrients = eutrophication.

questions.text: The greenhouse effect is mainly enhanced by an increase in the concentration of
questions.explanation:
Concept: The greenhouse effect is the trapping of heat by gases in the atmosphere.
Step 1: CO₂, CH₄, water vapour and N₂O absorb infrared radiation.
Step 2: Burning fossil fuels increases CO₂ in the air.
Step 3: More CO₂ means more heat trapped and global warming.
Answer: carbon(IV) oxide.
Common mistake: Nitrogen and argon do not absorb infrared radiation.
Similar example: Deforestation also raises CO₂ because fewer trees absorb it.
Tip: Greenhouse gas = absorbs infrared.

questions.text: Which of the following will turn blue litmus paper red?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue.
Step 1: HNO₃ is an acid, so it turns blue litmus red.
Step 2: NaOH, NH₃ and Ca(OH)₂ are bases and keep blue litmus blue.
Answer: Dilute HNO₃.
Similar example: Dilute HCl and ethanoic acid also turn blue litmus red.
Tip: Red = acid. Blue = base.

questions.text: A salt formed by incomplete replacement of the ionizable hydrogen ions of an acid is called
questions.explanation:
Concept: Salts can be normal, acid or basic, depending on how the acid's H⁺ or the base's OH⁻ are replaced.
Step 1: A dibasic acid like H₂SO₄ has two replaceable hydrogens.
Step 2: If only one is replaced, the salt still contains hydrogen: NaHSO₄.
Step 3: This is an acid salt.
Answer: an acid salt.
Common mistake: A normal salt has all replaceable hydrogens replaced, e.g. Na₂SO₄.
Similar example: NaHCO₃ is also an acid salt.
Tip: Contains H and still acidic: acid salt.

questions.text: The salt formed when sodium hydroxide reacts with excess carbon(IV) oxide is
questions.explanation:
Concept: The product depends on how much CO₂ reacts with NaOH.
Step 1: Limited CO₂: 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.
Step 2: Excess CO₂: Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → 2NaHCO₃.
Step 3: Overall: NaOH + CO₂ → NaHCO₃.
Answer: NaHCO₃.
Similar example: Excess CO₂ in lime water first forms a milky precipitate and then redissolves as Ca(HCO₃)₂.
Tip: Excess CO₂ gives the hydrogencarbonate.

questions.text: What mass of NaOH is needed to prepare 250 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ solution? [Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Mass = moles × molar mass. Moles = concentration × volume (dm³).
Step 1: Moles = 0.1 × 0.25 = 0.025 mol.
Step 2: Molar mass of NaOH = 40 g/mol.
Step 3: Mass = 0.025 × 40 = 1.0 g.
Answer: 1.0 g.
Common mistake: Using 250 instead of 0.25 dm³ gives a wrong answer.
Similar example: 500 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ NaOH needs 0.1 mol = 4.0 g.
Tip: Convert cm³ to dm³ first.

questions.text: In the reaction Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂, the substance oxidised is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain.
Step 1: Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻: bromide loses electrons and its oxidation number rises from −1 to 0.
Step 2: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻: chlorine is reduced.
Step 3: So Br⁻ is the substance oxidised.
Answer: Br⁻.
Common mistake: Cl₂ is the oxidising agent, not the substance oxidised.
Similar example: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, zinc is oxidised.
Tip: Oxidised = oxidation number increases.

questions.text: Which of the following is the strongest reducing agent?
questions.explanation:
Concept: A strong reducing agent loses electrons easily.
Step 1: Metals high in the reactivity series lose electrons easily.
Step 2: Potassium is very high in the series.
Step 3: Copper, silver and gold are poor reducing agents.
Answer: Potassium.
Similar example: Sodium and magnesium are also strong reducing agents.
Tip: Most reactive metal = strongest reducing agent.

questions.text: During the electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulphate using copper electrodes, the mass of the anode
questions.explanation:
Concept: In electrolysis of CuSO₄(aq) with copper electrodes, copper is transferred from anode to cathode.
Step 1: At the anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (copper dissolves).
Step 2: At the cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (copper deposits).
Step 3: The anode loses mass and the cathode gains mass.
Answer: decreases.
Similar example: This is how impure copper is refined.
Tip: Active electrode: anode dissolves.

questions.text: In the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, the product at the anode is
questions.explanation:
Concept: In electrolysis of a molten binary compound, the metal forms at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.
Step 1: PbBr₂ → Pb²⁺ + 2Br⁻.
Step 2: Cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb.
Step 3: Anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
Step 4: Bromine (a red-brown gas) is formed at the anode.
Answer: bromine.
Similar example: In molten NaCl, chlorine forms at the anode and sodium at the cathode.
Tip: Molten: only two ions, no water.

questions.text: The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is
questions.explanation:
Concept: The standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states.
Step 1: An element in its standard state is already 'formed'.
Step 2: So no energy change is involved.
Step 3: ΔHf° = 0 for elements such as O₂(g), H₂(g), C(graphite), Na(s).
Answer: zero.
Similar example: ΔHf° of O₂(g) is 0 but ΔHf° of O₃(g) is not zero, because O₂ is the standard form.
Tip: Elements: zero.

questions.text: The heat of neutralization of a strong acid and a strong base is about −57 kJ/mol because
options: the reaction is essentially H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
questions.explanation:
Concept: When a strong acid reacts with a strong base, both are fully ionized.
Step 1: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ and NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻.
Step 2: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions.
Step 3: The net reaction is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, with ΔH ≈ −57 kJ/mol.
Answer: the reaction is essentially H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
Common mistake: With a weak acid or weak base, some energy is used to ionize it, so ΔH is smaller in magnitude.
Similar example: HNO₃ with KOH also gives about −57 kJ/mol.
Tip: Strong + strong: same ΔH.

questions.text: In a reaction, the energy barrier that must be overcome for reactants to form products is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Activation energy (Eₐ) is the minimum energy colliding particles must have to react.
Step 1: On an energy profile, it is the height from the reactants to the top of the hill.
Step 2: ΔH is the difference between reactants and products.
Answer: activation energy.
Common mistake: Enthalpy of reaction (ΔH) is the overall energy difference. It is not the barrier.
Similar example: A catalyst lowers Eₐ but does not change ΔH.
Tip: Barrier = activation energy.

questions.text: Which of the following will NOT affect the rate of the reaction between zinc granules and dilute H₂SO₄?
options: Changing the colour of the container
questions.explanation:
Concept: Rate depends on temperature, concentration, surface area, catalyst and pressure (for gases).
Step 1: Higher temperature makes the reaction faster.
Step 2: A more concentrated acid makes it faster.
Step 3: Powdered zinc makes it faster.
Step 4: The colour of the container has no effect on the rate.
Answer: Changing the colour of the container.
Similar example: Light can affect some reactions (photochemical), but not the colour of the container.
Tip: Look for the factor that is not physical or chemical.

questions.text: In the reaction H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), increasing the pressure at constant temperature will
options: have no effect on the equilibrium position
shift the equilibrium to the right
shift the equilibrium to the left
questions.explanation:
Concept: The number of gas moles on each side decides whether pressure has an effect.
Step 1: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI: 2 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles on the right.
Step 2: Changing the pressure affects both sides equally.
Step 3: So the position of equilibrium does not change.
Answer: have no effect on the equilibrium position.
Common mistake: Kc depends on temperature only. Pressure never changes Kc.
Similar example: In 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄ pressure does matter because the moles change from 2 to 1.
Tip: Equal gas moles: pressure has no effect.

questions.text: If Kc for a reaction is very large, the equilibrium mixture contains mainly
options: equal amounts of reactants and products
questions.explanation:
Concept: Kc = [products] ÷ [reactants] at equilibrium.
Step 1: A very large Kc means the numerator is much larger than the denominator.
Step 2: So the equilibrium mixture is mostly products.
Step 3: The reaction goes almost to completion.
Answer: products.
Similar example: A very small Kc (e.g. 10⁻¹⁰) means the mixture is mostly reactants.
Tip: Large Kc: lots of products.

questions.text: Which of the following gases is collected by upward delivery?
questions.explanation:
Concept: The method of collecting a gas depends on its density and solubility.
Step 1: Chlorine (M = 71) is denser than air (M ≈ 29), so it is collected by upward delivery (downward displacement of air).
Step 2: Hydrogen, ammonia and methane are less dense than air and are collected by downward delivery (upward displacement of air).
Answer: Chlorine.
Similar example: CO₂ is also collected by upward delivery.
Tip: Heavier than air: upward delivery.

questions.text: Hydrogen sulphide gas can be identified by its
options: pungent smell and turning red litmus blue
rotten-egg smell and its blackening of lead(II) ethanoate paper
questions.explanation:
Concept: H₂S is a toxic gas with a characteristic smell.
Step 1: It smells like rotten eggs.
Step 2: Test: paper soaked in lead(II) ethanoate turns black.
Step 3: Pb²⁺ + S²⁻ → PbS (black).
Answer: rotten-egg smell and its blackening of lead(II) ethanoate paper.
Similar example: H₂S is prepared by adding dilute HCl to iron(II) sulphide.
Tip: Black PbS: sulphide present.

questions.text: Iron is protected from rusting by coating with zinc. This process is called
questions.explanation:
Concept: Galvanization coats iron or steel with a layer of zinc.
Step 1: Zinc is more reactive than iron.
Step 2: It acts as a barrier and also corrodes in preference to iron (sacrificial protection).
Step 3: Even a scratch in the layer does not expose the iron to rusting.
Answer: galvanization.
Common mistake: Anodization is for aluminium, vulcanization is for rubber, and pasteurization is for milk.
Similar example: Corrugated roofing sheets are galvanized.
Tip: Zinc on iron: galvanization.

questions.text: Which of the following ions gives a white precipitate with NaOH(aq) that dissolves in excess NaOH(aq) and also in excess NH₃(aq)?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Zinc hydroxide is amphoteric, so it dissolves in both excess NaOH and excess NH₃.
Step 1: Zn²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Zn(OH)₂ (white precipitate).
Step 2: Excess NaOH gives soluble zincate, [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻.
Step 3: Excess NH₃ gives soluble [Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺.
Answer: Zn²⁺.
Common mistake: Pb²⁺ also gives a white precipitate soluble in excess NaOH but not in excess NH₃.
Similar example: Ca²⁺ gives a white precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH.
Tip: Zn²⁺: soluble in both.

questions.text: The addition of hydrogen to an unsaturated vegetable oil in the presence of nickel is known as
questions.explanation:
Concept: Hydrogenation adds hydrogen to the C=C bonds of an unsaturated compound.
Step 1: Vegetable oil + H₂ (nickel catalyst, about 180°C) → saturated fat.
Step 2: This raises the melting point, turning liquid oil into a solid fat.
Step 3: Margarine is made this way.
Answer: hydrogenation.
Similar example: Ethene + H₂ → ethane is also hydrogenation.
Tip: Oil to margarine: hydrogenation.

questions.text: The compound CH₃COOC₂H₅ is an
questions.explanation:
Concept: Esters have the functional group –COO– and are formed from an acid and an alcohol.
Step 1: CH₃COOC₂H₅ comes from CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid) and C₂H₅OH (ethanol).
Step 2: Its name is ethyl ethanoate.
Answer: ester.
Similar example: CH₃COOCH₃ is methyl ethanoate.
Tip: Name = alcohol part first, then acid part.

questions.text: Which of the following is the most suitable method of obtaining pure water from sea water?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Distillation separates a solvent from the dissolved solids by boiling and condensing.
Step 1: Heat the sea water until the water boils.
Step 2: The steam is cooled in a condenser and collected as pure water.
Step 3: The dissolved salts stay behind in the flask.
Answer: Distillation.
Common mistake: Filtration cannot remove dissolved salt, because dissolved particles pass through filter paper.
Similar example: Distillation is also used to make distilled water in the laboratory.
Tip: Dissolved solid + solvent wanted: distillation.

questions.text: A mixture of iron filings and sulphur can be separated by
questions.explanation:
Concept: Iron is attracted by a magnet, but sulphur is not.
Step 1: Spread the mixture out and pass a magnet over it.
Step 2: Iron filings stick to the magnet.
Step 3: Sulphur remains.
Answer: using a magnet.
Similar example: A mixture of iron filings and sand is separated the same way.
Tip: Magnetic substances: Fe, Co, Ni.

questions.text: In the compound Fe₂O₃, the percentage by mass of iron is [Fe = 56, O = 16]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Percentage by mass = (mass of the element ÷ molar mass of the compound) × 100.
Step 1: Molar mass of Fe₂O₃ = 2(56) + 3(16) = 112 + 48 = 160.
Step 2: Mass of Fe = 112.
Step 3: % Fe = 112/160 × 100 = 70%.
Answer: 70%.
Common mistake: Do not use 56 only. There are two iron atoms in each formula unit.
Similar example: % of Mg in MgO = 24/40 × 100 = 60%.
Tip: Multiply atomic mass by the number of atoms.

questions.text: The molecular formula of a compound with empirical formula CH₂O and relative molecular mass 180 is [C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Molecular formula = (empirical formula)ₙ, where n = molecular mass ÷ empirical mass.
Step 1: Empirical mass of CH₂O = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30.
Step 2: n = 180 ÷ 30 = 6.
Step 3: Molecular formula = (CH₂O)₆ = C₆H₁₂O₆.
Answer: C₆H₁₂O₆.
Similar example: Empirical formula CH with M = 78: empirical mass 13, n = 6, so C₆H₆.
Tip: Multiply every subscript by n.

questions.text: What volume of hydrogen at s.t.p. is liberated when 0.1 mol of magnesium reacts with excess dilute HCl? [Molar volume = 22.4 dm³]
questions.explanation:
Concept: Use mole ratios from the balanced equation and 22.4 dm³ per mole at s.t.p.
Step 1: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.
Step 2: 1 mol Mg gives 1 mol H₂, so 0.1 mol Mg gives 0.1 mol H₂.
Step 3: Volume = 0.1 × 22.4 = 2.24 dm³.
Answer: 2.24 dm³.
Common mistake: Using 22.4 dm³ for 0.1 mol is wrong. Multiply by the moles.
Similar example: 0.5 mol of Zn gives 0.5 × 22.4 = 11.2 dm³ of H₂.
Tip: Moles of gas × 22.4 = volume at s.t.p.

questions.text: What volume of oxygen at s.t.p. is needed for complete combustion of 5 dm³ of methane, CH₄?
questions.explanation:
Concept: For gases at the same temperature and pressure, volume ratios equal mole ratios.
Step 1: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
Step 2: 1 volume of CH₄ needs 2 volumes of O₂.
Step 3: 5 dm³ of CH₄ needs 5 × 2 = 10 dm³ of O₂.
Answer: 10 dm³.
Similar example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: 10 dm³ of H₂ needs 5 dm³ of O₂.
Tip: Coefficients are also volume ratios for gases.

questions.text: Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes states that gases combine in volumes that
options: are in simple whole-number ratios at the same temperature and pressure
questions.explanation:
Concept: Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes links reacting gas volumes.
Step 1: When gases react, their volumes are in simple whole-number ratios.
Step 2: This applies at the same temperature and pressure.
Answer: are in simple whole-number ratios at the same temperature and pressure.
Similar example: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl: volumes are in the ratio 1 : 1 : 2.
Tip: Law of combining volumes = gas volumes.

questions.text: The temperature at which the volume of an ideal gas would theoretically be zero is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature, where an ideal gas would have zero volume.
Step 1: 0 K corresponds to −273°C.
Step 2: K = °C + 273.
Answer: −273°C.
Similar example: 0°C = 273 K and 100°C = 373 K.
Tip: Absolute zero: 0 K = −273°C.

questions.text: A gas at 3 atm and 300 K occupies 2 dm³. What will be its pressure if the volume is increased to 6 dm³ at the same temperature?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ at constant temperature.
Step 1: P₁ = 3 atm, V₁ = 2 dm³, V₂ = 6 dm³.
Step 2: P₂ = (3 × 2) ÷ 6.
Step 3: P₂ = 1 atm.
Answer: 1 atm.
Common mistake: Temperature is given but constant here, so no conversion to kelvin is needed.
Similar example: A gas at 4 atm and 1 dm³ is expanded to 8 dm³ giving 0.5 atm.
Tip: Volume × 3 means pressure ÷ 3.

questions.text: The atomic number of an element is 15. Its valence electron configuration is
questions.explanation:
Concept: The electronic configuration is built from the atomic number.
Step 1: Z = 15: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p³.
Step 2: The valence shell is the third shell: 3s²3p³.
Step 3: This is phosphorus with 5 valence electrons.
Answer: 3s²3p³.
Similar example: Z = 16 (sulphur): 3s²3p⁴.
Tip: Valence electrons = outer s and p electrons.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a coordinate (dative) covalent bond compound?
questions.explanation:
Concept: A dative (coordinate) bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons come from the same atom.
Step 1: In H₃O⁺, oxygen has lone pairs.
Step 2: One lone pair is donated to H⁺, which has no electrons.
Step 3: This forms a dative bond.
Answer: H₃O⁺.
Common mistake: CH₄ and H₂ have normal covalent bonds, and NaCl is ionic.
Similar example: NH₄⁺ also contains a dative bond.
Tip: Lone pair + empty orbital = dative bond.

questions.text: The sub-atomic particle that determines the chemical properties of an element is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The behaviour of an atom in a reaction depends on its outer electrons.
Step 1: Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to complete the outer shell.
Step 2: Protons fix the identity of the element but electrons decide how it reacts.
Answer: electron.
Similar example: Elements in the same group have similar chemistry because they have the same number of valence electrons.
Tip: Chemistry = electrons.

questions.text: Which of the following types of radiation has the highest penetrating power?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Radiation differs in penetrating power.
Step 1: Alpha particles are stopped by paper.
Step 2: Beta particles are stopped by thin aluminium.
Step 3: Gamma rays are stopped only by thick lead or concrete.
Answer: Gamma rays.
Similar example: Ionizing power is highest for alpha and lowest for gamma.
Tip: Penetration: γ > β > α.

questions.text: The half-life of a radioactive element is 10 days. What fraction of the original amount remains after 30 days?
questions.explanation:
Concept: After each half-life, the amount remaining is halved.
Step 1: Number of half-lives = 30 ÷ 10 = 3.
Step 2: Fraction left = (1/2)³ = 1/8.
Answer: 1/8.
Common mistake: A fraction of 1/6 is wrong. Halve repeatedly.
Similar example: After 20 days (2 half-lives), 1/4 remains.
Tip: n half-lives: (1/2)ⁿ.

questions.text: Which of the following substances is NOT a mixture?
questions.explanation:
Concept: A pure substance has one component. A mixture contains two or more substances not chemically combined.
Step 1: Air, sea water and brass are mixtures.
Step 2: Distilled water is H₂O only, so it is pure.
Answer: Distilled water.
Similar example: Brass is a mixture (alloy) of copper and zinc.
Tip: Look for a single compound or element.

questions.text: The percentage by volume of oxygen in dry air is approximately
questions.explanation:
Concept: Dry air is about 78% N₂, 21% O₂ and 1% other gases by volume.
Step 1: Oxygen forms about 21% of dry air.
Step 2: This fraction supports burning and respiration.
Answer: 21%.
Similar example: Burning a candle in a closed jar uses up about one-fifth of the air.
Tip: Remember 78 : 21 : 1.

questions.text: Which of the following is used to remove carbon(IV) oxide from air in the laboratory?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Acidic gases such as CO₂ are absorbed by an alkali.
Step 1: CO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.
Step 2: Concentrated NaOH removes CO₂ from the air.
Step 3: CaCl₂ and H₂SO₄ only remove water vapour.
Answer: Concentrated NaOH solution.
Similar example: Soda lime (NaOH + CaO) is used in breathing apparatus to absorb CO₂.
Tip: CO₂ is acidic, so use an alkali.

questions.text: Which of the following can be used to remove temporary hardness of water?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Temporary hardness is caused by hydrogencarbonates of calcium and magnesium.
Step 1: Boiling: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O + CO₂.
Step 2: The insoluble CaCO₃ settles as scale.
Step 3: The water becomes soft.
Answer: Boiling.
Common mistake: Boiling does not remove permanent hardness (sulphates and chlorides).
Similar example: Kettle scale is CaCO₃ from temporary hard water.
Tip: Boil away temporary hardness.

questions.text: What mass of KNO₃ will dissolve in 200 g of water at 40°C if its solubility is 60 g per 100 g of water?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Solubility is the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of water.
Step 1: 60 g dissolves in 100 g of water.
Step 2: 200 g is twice 100 g.
Step 3: Mass dissolved = 60 × 2 = 120 g.
Answer: 120 g.
Similar example: If 30 g dissolves in 100 g of water, then 50 g of water dissolves 15 g.
Tip: Scale by the amount of water.

questions.text: Which of the following compounds is least soluble in water?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Solubility rules help you recall which salts are insoluble.
Step 1: All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble.
Step 2: All nitrates are soluble.
Step 3: Chlorides are soluble except AgCl, PbCl₂ and Hg₂Cl₂.
Step 4: So AgCl is the least soluble.
Answer: AgCl.
Similar example: BaSO₄ and PbSO₄ are insoluble sulphates.
Tip: AgCl is a white precipitate.

questions.text: The release of oil into the sea mainly causes
options: death of aquatic life by cutting off oxygen supply
questions.explanation:
Concept: Oil on water forms a film on the surface.
Step 1: The film reduces the amount of oxygen dissolving in water.
Step 2: It blocks sunlight, reducing photosynthesis.
Step 3: Fish and other aquatic life die.
Answer: death of aquatic life by cutting off oxygen supply.
Similar example: Seabirds are also harmed because oil coats their feathers.
Tip: Oil spills damage aquatic ecosystems.

questions.text: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are mainly responsible for
questions.explanation:
Concept: CFCs are stable compounds used in refrigerators and aerosols.
Step 1: In the stratosphere, UV light breaks C–Cl bonds and releases chlorine atoms.
Step 2: Each chlorine atom destroys many ozone molecules.
Step 3: The ozone layer becomes thinner.
Answer: depletion of the ozone layer.
Common mistake: Acid rain is caused by SO₂ and NOₓ, not CFCs.
Similar example: The Montreal Protocol was designed to phase out CFCs.
Tip: CFC = ozone depletion.

questions.text: The pH of a 0.01 mol/dm³ solution of the strong base NaOH is
questions.explanation:
Concept: For a strong base, [OH⁻] equals the concentration of the base.
Step 1: [OH⁻] = 0.01 = 10⁻² mol/dm³.
Step 2: pOH = 2.
Step 3: pH = 14 − 2 = 12.
Answer: 12.
Common mistake: Giving a pH of 2 is the common error. That would be an acid of the same concentration.
Similar example: 0.001 mol/dm³ NaOH gives pH 11.
Tip: Base: pH = 14 − pOH.

questions.text: Which of the following is a weak acid?
questions.explanation:
Concept: A weak acid ionizes only partly in water.
Step 1: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (only a small fraction ionizes).
Step 2: HCl, HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ are strong acids and ionize completely.
Answer: CH₃COOH.
Similar example: Carbonic acid and citric acid are also weak acids.
Tip: Organic acids are usually weak.

questions.text: 20 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl neutralizes 25 cm³ of NaOH solution. The concentration of the NaOH is
questions.explanation:
Concept: At the end point, moles of acid = moles of base for a 1 : 1 reaction.
Step 1: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
Step 2: Moles HCl = 0.1 × 0.020 = 0.002 mol.
Step 3: Moles NaOH = 0.002 mol in 25 cm³ = 0.025 dm³.
Step 4: [NaOH] = 0.002 ÷ 0.025 = 0.08 mol/dm³.
Answer: 0.08 mol/dm³.
Common mistake: Using the formula C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ also works for 1 : 1 reactions: 0.1 × 20 = C × 25, so C = 0.08.
Similar example: 25 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ HCl needs 25 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ NaOH.
Tip: 1 : 1 ratio: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂.

questions.text: The oxidation number of nitrogen in NH₄⁺ is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Oxidation number rules: ions have oxidation numbers equal to the charge, and hydrogen is usually +1.
Step 1: Let N = x in NH₄⁺.
Step 2: x + 4(+1) = +1.
Step 3: x = −3.
Answer: −3.
Similar example: In NO₃⁻: x + 3(−2) = −1 gives N = +5.
Tip: Sum = charge of the ion.

questions.text: Which of the following is a disproportionation reaction?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Disproportionation: one species is both oxidised and reduced in the same reaction.
Step 1: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O.
Step 2: Cl goes from 0 to −1 (reduction) in NaCl.
Step 3: Cl goes from 0 to +1 (oxidation) in NaOCl.
Step 4: The same element (Cl) does both.
Answer: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O.
Similar example: H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂ is another disproportionation.
Tip: One element, oxidised and reduced.

questions.text: The substance deposited at the cathode when aqueous copper(II) sulphate is electrolysed with platinum electrodes is
questions.explanation:
Concept: In electrolysis of aqueous CuSO₄ with inert electrodes, the less reactive cation is discharged.
Step 1: Ions present: Cu²⁺, H⁺, SO₄²⁻, OH⁻.
Step 2: Cu²⁺ is lower than H⁺ in the electrochemical series.
Step 3: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu is deposited at the cathode.
Answer: copper.
Similar example: In aqueous NaCl, hydrogen is liberated at the cathode because H⁺ is below Na⁺.
Tip: Cathode: choose the less reactive metal.

questions.text: The mass of silver deposited by 0.5 faraday of electricity from Ag⁺ solution is [Ag = 108]
questions.explanation:
Concept: 1 faraday deposits 1 mole of a monovalent metal.
Step 1: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag. 1 F deposits 1 mol = 108 g.
Step 2: 0.5 F deposits 0.5 mol = 54 g.
Answer: 54 g.
Similar example: 0.5 F deposits 0.25 mol of Cu²⁺ (Cu = 63.5) = 15.9 g.
Tip: Mass = (Q ÷ 96,500) × molar mass ÷ charge.

questions.text: The reaction in which heat is absorbed from the surroundings is described as
questions.explanation:
Concept: Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings (ΔH is positive).
Step 1: The products have higher enthalpy than the reactants.
Step 2: The surroundings get cooler.
Answer: endothermic.
Similar example: Photosynthesis and dissolving ammonium nitrate are endothermic.
Tip: Endo = in.

questions.text: When 2 g of NaOH dissolve in water, the temperature rises. This shows that dissolution of NaOH is
questions.explanation:
Concept: A rise in temperature when a substance dissolves means heat is given out.
Step 1: NaOH dissolves and the solution warms up.
Step 2: Heat flows from the system to the surroundings.
Step 3: So the dissolution is exothermic.
Answer: exothermic.
Similar example: Dissolving NH₄Cl lowers the temperature, so it is endothermic.
Tip: Temperature up: exothermic.

questions.text: The unit of the rate constant of a first-order reaction is
questions.explanation:
Concept: The unit of k depends on the order of the reaction.
Step 1: First order: rate = k[A].
Step 2: k = rate/[A] = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) ÷ (mol dm⁻³).
Step 3: k has the unit s⁻¹.
Answer: s⁻¹.
Similar example: Second order: k has unit dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Tip: First order: s⁻¹.

questions.text: In the reaction N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), an increase in pressure
questions.explanation:
Concept: Increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas moles.
Step 1: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂: 1 mole of gas on the left and 2 moles on the right.
Step 2: High pressure favours the left side.
Step 3: The equilibrium shifts left.
Answer: shifts equilibrium to the left.
Common mistake: Pressure does not change Kc. Only temperature does.
Similar example: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ shifts right with increased pressure (3 moles → 2).
Tip: Fewer moles = favoured at high pressure.

questions.text: Ammonia is manufactured by the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Haber process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
Step 1: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
Step 2: Conditions: iron catalyst, about 450°C and 200 atm.
Step 3: Contact process makes H₂SO₄, Solvay makes Na₂CO₃ and Ostwald makes HNO₃.
Answer: Haber process.
Similar example: Most ammonia goes into fertilizers.
Tip: Haber = ammonia.

questions.text: The gas produced when copper reacts with concentrated trioxonitrate(V) acid is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Concentrated nitric acid is an oxidising agent.
Step 1: Cu + 4HNO₃(conc) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O.
Step 2: The gas is brown nitrogen(IV) oxide.
Step 3: Dilute HNO₃ gives NO instead.
